# About Conyso Publishing

> Why Conyso Publishing exists, what it publishes, how it is connected to Conyso, and who edits its books: Krishna Chagti, the founder of Conyso.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/about.html

About the imprint

# About Conyso Publishing

A small imprint with one rule: a book should check the story before it tells it.

## Why does it exist?

Conyso built the Law Tome and the Bias Atlas as free, sourced references: what each named law or bias says, where it came from, and how well it holds up. Working on them turned up the same thing again and again. Many of the famous stories attached to these ideas are wrong, misattributed or still argued over, and the correct versions are often better stories.

Conyso Publishing exists to put those findings into books people actually pick up: a quiz for the dinner table, a reference for the shelf. The datasets stay free online. The books are the edited, designed, offline version.

## What does it publish?

Quiz and reference books in two series, one for each dataset. The first title is [*True or Folklore?*](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore.html), 100 famous stories put to the test, coming soon in paperback and Kindle. [The series page](https://conyso.com/publishing/series.html) explains how a dataset becomes a series.

## How is it connected to Conyso?

Conyso Publishing is Conyso's imprint, the name on the spine of its books. Conyso publishes the two datasets the books are built from, and the books link back to them: every answer names its source and points to the record it comes from. [Conyso's home page](https://conyso.com/index.html) has the rest of the company.

## Who is the editor?

Krishna Chagti founded Conyso, which publishes the Law Tome and the Bias Atlas, and he edits the books built from them. He chooses what goes into each book, reads and approves the finished book before it goes on sale, and is the name on its cover: the books are credited to him as editor, not to an invented author.

His other work, from Conyso's ventures to his research papers, is on [his founder site](https://conyso.com/founder/).

## How do you report a mistake?

Every book prints the address of its [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/) in the front matter. A mistake found after print goes there, with what changed. [How corrections work](https://conyso.com/publishing/standards.html#corrections) is in our standards.

# How we make books

> The nine steps from a sourced record to a printed book, and the seven checks every Conyso Publishing title must pass before it goes on sale.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/how-we-make-books.html

The process

# How we make books

From a sourced record to a printed page, with a check at every step that can go wrong.

## What are the steps?

1. Choose the entriesA book starts from a brief and an outline: which records go in, in what order, for which reader. For a quiz book that means a story with a version almost everyone knows and a record that can be checked.
2. Draft from the recordThe text is drafted with AI from the dataset's record, which carries the claim, its history and its sources. The draft may only say what the record supports.
3. Check every verdictEvery verdict, quote and date is checked against a primary source, or the best one available. Each check is logged with what was opened, the date, and whether the draft held, was fixed or was flagged. A flagged verdict waits for the editor.
4. Read for living peopleAny entry that names a living person gets a legal wording pass before print.
5. Make and review the artIllustrations are made with AI, then every image is checked against a twelve-point list and a second reviewer looks at the full set.
6. Rewrite anything too closeThe manuscript is compared with the Wikipedia articles it cites, and any non-quoted run of twelve or more shared words is rewritten.
7. Typeset and proofThe book is typeset, run through a manuscript checker, and proofed in print.
8. Editor approvalThe editor reads the final file and the cover and approves them. Nothing goes on sale without that, because the book goes out in his name.
9. Publish and discloseThe book goes on sale with the store's AI-generated box ticked for both text and images, and its corrections page already live.

## What has to be true before a book ships?

Seven checks. If any one fails, the book slips a week rather than going out with a gap.

1. The manuscript checker passes.
2. Every factual claim is traced to a source in the record, and every verdict and quote is checked and logged.
3. The legal wording pass on living people is done.
4. Every image passes the twelve-point list, and a second reviewer has seen the full set.
5. The cover, description, keywords and categories are written, with the AI disclosure ready.
6. Every web address printed in the book works.
7. The editor has approved the final file and cover.

## What does that look like in a real book?

In [*True or Folklore?*](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore.html), eight of the hundred stories had a verdict the source check flagged for an editor's decision, and they are being settled before print. Round 1 is online with each story's check: what was opened, and when. [Play it and see](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore-round-1.html).

## Questions about the process

How long does a book take?

Each book moves through five stages over about three weeks: brief and outline, draft and art, checks, approval, then publication. Several books are worked on at once.

What stops a book from shipping?

Any one of seven checks failing. The book slips a week rather than going out with a gap.

Where are the sources?

A short source line sits on each entry in the book, and the full list is on the matching Law Tome or Bias Atlas entry online.


======================================================================

# How we use AI

> What AI does in a Conyso Publishing book (drafts the text, makes the art), what is checked around it, and what we disclose on every title.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/how-we-use-ai.html

Disclosure

# How we use AI

Plainly: AI drafts the text and makes the pictures. Here is what happens around that.

## What does AI do?

- **Drafts the text** of each entry from the dataset's record: the claim, its history and its sources.
- **Makes the illustrations**, such as the cartoons in *True or Folklore?*

## What happens around the AI?

- **The record comes first.** A draft may only say what a sourced record supports.
- **Every verdict is checked** against a primary source, or the best available, and the check is logged with what was opened and when. In the free round you can see each story's check.
- **Flagged verdicts wait.** If the check finds a problem it cannot settle, the story waits for the editor.
- **Living people get a legal read.**
- **Every image is reviewed** against a twelve-point list, and a second reviewer sees the full set.
- **The editor approves** the final book and cover.

## What do we disclose, and where?

The store's AI-generated box is ticked for both text and images on every title. Every page of this site carries a one-line disclosure in its footer, and each book's front matter says how it was made. The books are credited to a real editor, not an invented author.

## What if the AI got something wrong?

Then it is our mistake, and it goes on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/) printed in the book. [Our standards](https://conyso.com/publishing/standards.html) say how corrections work.

## Questions about AI

Is the book written by AI?

The text is drafted with AI from sourced records, and the illustrations are made with AI. The checking, the legal read and the editor's approval sit on top of that draft, and the store listing says so.

Does the AI decide the verdicts?

The draft states the verdict the record supports. Every verdict is then checked against its sources and the check is logged; a verdict the check flags waits for the editor, and the editor approves the finished book.

Why use AI at all?

Because it makes it possible to turn a large sourced dataset into many short entries, and to spend the human time on choosing, checking and correcting instead.

# Conyso Publishing

An imprint of Conyso

# Conyso Publishing

Quiz and reference books built from sourced records. Checked before print. Corrected in public.

SOURCED · CHECKED · CORRECTED

[Play a free round](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore-round-1.html) [See book 1](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore.html)

![The cover of True or Folklore?, book 1](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/cover.png)

Book 1 · Coming soon

## What does Conyso Publishing publish?

Books that take a famous claim and check it: the named laws people quote, the stories told about how they were found, and the thinking errors that make the stories stick.

Conyso keeps two free reference sets online. [The Law Tome](https://conyso.com/lawtome/) covers 1,116 named laws, effects and principles: the laws of science and everyday life, like Murphy's law or Newton's, not legal statutes. [The Bias Atlas](https://conyso.com/biases/) covers 544 cognitive biases and which findings held up. Every entry in both names its sources. The imprint turns those records into books for a game night, a classroom or a shelf. The datasets stay free; the books are what you read away from a screen.

## How is a book made?

1. **1**From a recordEvery entry starts from a Law Tome or Bias Atlas record, which names its sources.
2. **2**Drafted, then checkedAI drafts the text from the record. Every verdict, quote and date is checked against the sources, and the check is logged.
3. **3**Signed offLiving people get a legal read, the art is reviewed by two people, and the editor approves the final book.
4. **4**Corrected in publicEvery book prints the address of its corrections page. Mistakes found later go there.

[The full process](https://conyso.com/publishing/how-we-make-books.html) [How we use AI](https://conyso.com/publishing/how-we-use-ai.html)

## Questions about the imprint

What is Conyso Publishing?

Conyso's imprint for quiz and reference books. Every book is built from one of Conyso's free, sourced datasets, [the Law Tome](https://conyso.com/lawtome/) or [the Bias Atlas](https://conyso.com/biases/), and checked against the sources before print.

Who is behind it?

Conyso, the company that publishes the two datasets. The books are edited by [Krishna Chagti](https://conyso.com/publishing/about.html#editor), Conyso's founder.

Are the books written by AI?

The text is drafted with AI from the sourced records, and the illustrations are made with AI. Every verdict is then checked against its sources and the check is logged, and the editor approves the finished book. [How we use AI](https://conyso.com/publishing/how-we-use-ai.html) has the detail.

Which books are out?

None yet. The first, [*True or Folklore?*](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore.html), is coming soon in paperback and Kindle. Its first round is free to play here.

How do I report a mistake?

Corrections are listed on the [public corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/), which every book prints in its front matter.

# Two series, two datasets

> Conyso Publishing's two series: books built from the Law Tome's 1,116 named laws and from the Bias Atlas's 544 cognitive biases.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/series.html

The series

# Two series, two datasets

Every Conyso Publishing book belongs to the dataset it is built from.

Series one

## The Law Tome series

Built from [the Law Tome](https://conyso.com/lawtome/), a free directory of 1,116 named laws, effects and principles. Each law there has what it says, who it is named after, where it came from and how well it holds up, with sources. The books in this series take that record somewhere a screen can't go: a dinner table, a quiz night, a classroom.

![The cover of True or Folklore?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/cover.png)

The Law Tome series · Book 1 · Coming soon

### True or Folklore?

100 Famous Stories You've Been Told Wrong: The Myth-Busting Quiz for Curious Minds

Series two

## The Bias Atlas series

Built from [the Bias Atlas](https://conyso.com/biases/), a free map of 544 cognitive biases: what each one is, how to spot it, and whether the research behind it held up. No titles are announced yet. They will be listed here when they are ready.

## How does a dataset become a series?

A series keeps the dataset's habits. Each entry names its source, links back to its record online, and goes through the same checks. The record is the source of truth: when a book and its record disagree, the record is checked again and one of them is corrected.


======================================================================

# Our standards

> What our verdicts mean, how sources and living people are handled, what we will never do to sell a book, and how corrections work.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/standards.html

Publishing principles

# Our standards

The rules every Conyso Publishing book follows, written down so you can hold us to them.

## What do the verdicts mean?

TRUE

The record supports the story as usually told.

FOLKLORE

The famous version is wrong, misattributed or added later, and the record shows what really happened.

DISPUTED

Good sources disagree, or the evidence is not there to settle it. We say so rather than pick a side.

## How are sources handled?

Every entry names its source on the page, with the earliest source that settles the question where one exists. The full list sits on the matching Law Tome or Bias Atlas entry online. Every verdict is checked against a primary source, or the best one available, and the check is logged. Where the check cannot settle a verdict, the story waits.

Wording is our own: any non-quoted run of twelve or more words shared with a cited Wikipedia article is rewritten.

## How are living people treated?

Any entry that names a living person gets a legal wording pass before print. Criticism is attributed to the named source that makes it, and claims about a person's motives are left out.

## What will we never do?

- NEVERInvent a source, a quote, a date or a number.
- NEVERFake scarcity, countdowns or "was" prices. A print-on-demand book never runs out.
- NEVERBuy, swap or gate reviews, or route only happy readers to a store.
- NEVERCall a book a bestseller, or put other authors' names in our titles.
- NEVERPre-tick add-ons, shame a reader for saying no, or hide a subscription.
- NEVERCite effects that failed to replicate as if they had not.
- NEVERClaim social proof we do not have. Until there is real data, a myth is "widely believed", never "what most people think".

## What about reviews?

One neutral request at the end of a book, the same for every reader. Nothing is offered in exchange, and no reader is sorted by how happy they seem before being asked.

## How do corrections work?

Every book prints the address of its [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/) in the front matter. When a mistake is found, the correction goes there with what changed, and the next printing and the ebook are fixed. A correction is not hidden or quietly edited away.

Source: https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore-round-1.html

True or Folklore? · Free sample · Round 1 of 10

# Round 1: Famous scenes

The stories everyone has heard. A warm-up. Make your call on each story, then see the verdict and the sources it was checked against.

Your score

–

Make a call to start

Playing at a table?

Read each question aloud. Everyone writes TRUE, FOLKLORE or DISPUTED before anyone taps. One point for each right call; DISPUTED only scores if the call was DISPUTED. The book has a two-team scoresheet for this.

Print this round Share your score Copied Questions first, then an answer key on its own page.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/001.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 1

### Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?

**Folklore.** Archimedes stated the law of buoyancy around 250 BC, in his treatise *On Floating Bodies*. The bath, the crown and the cry of "Eureka!" are almost certainly a later embellishment.

Tell someone: Archimedes did state the law of buoyancy, but the bath and the "Eureka!" almost certainly come from Vitruvius, writing some two centuries later.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Vitruvius, Gwilt translation, LacusCurtius](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Vitruvius/9*.html)
- [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-archimede/)
- [Rorres, NYU](https://www.math.nyu.edu/~crorres/Archimedes/Crown/CrownIntro.html)

Cited in the book: Vitruvius, *De architectura*, book IX, preface. "Fact or Fiction?: Archimedes Coined the Term 'Eureka!' in the Bath," *Scientific American*. Rorres, "The Golden Crown," NYU. "Archimedes' principle," Wikipedia.

![Cartoon for the question: Did an apple fall on Newton's head?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/002.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 2

### Did an apple fall on Newton's head?

**Folklore.** There is an apple in Newton's own account of his thinking about gravity. It does not hit him on the head. That detail is a later embellishment.

Tell someone: According to *Britannica*, Newton's own recollection includes an apple but no bump; the hit on the head was a later embellishment.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Stukeley transcription, physics.info](https://physics.info/gravitation/quote-newton.shtml)
- [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/observations/whats-the-real-story-with-newton-and-the-apple-see-for-yourself/)

Cited in the book: Stukeley, *Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life* (1752). "Newton's law of gravitation," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. "Newton's law of universal gravitation," Wikipedia.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Newton himself tell the apple story?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/003.png)

TRUE

Round 1 · No. 3

### Did Newton himself tell the apple story?

**True.** The apple story is not a fable invented by Newton's admirers. According to *Encyclopaedia Britannica*, it traces back to Newton's own later recollection. Only the apple hitting his head was added afterward.

Tell someone: Newton himself told of the apple, according to *Britannica*; only the bump on the head was added later.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Stukeley transcription, physics.info](https://physics.info/gravitation/quote-newton.shtml)
- [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/observations/whats-the-real-story-with-newton-and-the-apple-see-for-yourself/)
- ["Discovery of Neptune," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_of_Neptune)

Cited in the book: Stukeley, *Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life* (1752). "Newton's law of gravitation," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. "Newton's law of universal gravitation," Wikipedia.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/004.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 4

### Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?

**Folklore.** The tower drop is likely a legend. It is not in Galileo's own writings. His documented work on falling bodies used balls rolling down ramps, with notes from around 1603 to 1604 and results published in 1638.

Tell someone: The tower drop is likely a legend; Galileo's documented work on falling bodies rolled balls down ramps and timed them with a water clock.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Galileo's Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo%27s_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment)
- ["Two New Sciences," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_New_Sciences)

Cited in the book: "Galileo's Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment," Wikipedia. "Two New Sciences," Wikipedia.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/005.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 5

### Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem?

**Folklore.** The relation that carries Pythagoras's name was known and used long before him. A Babylonian tablet from around 1800 BC lists its number triples, and Pythagoras lived from about 570 to 495 BC.

Tell someone: A Babylonian tablet from around 1800 BC already lists Pythagorean triples, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras was born.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Plimpton 322," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plimpton_322)
- ["Pythagorean theorem," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_theorem)

Cited in the book: "Pythagorean theorem," *Encyclopaedia Britannica*. "Pythagorean theorem," Wikipedia.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Einstein write E = mc² in his 1905 paper?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/006.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 6

### Did Einstein write E = mc² in his 1905 paper?

**Folklore.** Einstein's 1905 paper contains the idea but not the famous formula. It states in a single sentence that a body which gives off energy as radiation loses mass in proportion.

Tell someone: Look for E = mc² in Einstein's 1905 paper and it isn't there: he set out the mass-energy relation in a sentence.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Einstein (1905), English translation, fourmilab](https://www.fourmilab.ch/etexts/einstein/E_mc2/www/)

Cited in the book: Einstein, "Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?" (1905), English translation. "Mass-energy equivalence," Wikipedia.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/007.png)

TRUE

Round 1 · No. 7

### Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity?

**True.** Einstein's Nobel Prize, the physics prize designated for 1921, was for his work on the photoelectric effect. NobelPrize.org gives the citation as "for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect." Relativity is not what the prize named.

Tell someone: Einstein's Nobel was not for relativity: the prize designated for 1921 named his law of the photoelectric effect.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [NobelPrize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1921/summary/)
- [APS Physics 18, 12](https://physics.aps.org/articles/v18/12)
- [APS Historic Sites](https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/history/historicsites/millikan.cfm)

Cited in the book: Einstein, *Annalen der Physik* 322(6) (1905). The Nobel Prize in Physics 1921, NobelPrize.org. "Millikan's Measurement of Planck's Constant," APS Physics. "Robert Millikan," APS Historic Sites. "Photoelectric effect," Wikipedia.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Gordon Moore say chips double every 18 months?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/008.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 8

### Did Gordon Moore say chips double every 18 months?

**Folklore.** Gordon Moore never gave 18 months. His 1965 article predicted that the number of components on a chip would double roughly every year, and in 1975 he revised that to every two years.

Tell someone: Gordon Moore predicted a doubling roughly every year in 1965 and every two years in 1975; the 18 months was David House's.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Computer History Museum](https://www.computerhistory.org/siliconengine/moores-law-predicts-the-future-of-integrated-circuits/)
- ["Moore's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%27s_law)

Cited in the book: Moore, "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits," *Electronics* 38(8) (19 April 1965). "Moore's law," Wikipedia. Computer History Museum, "1965: 'Moore's Law' Predicts the Future of Integrated Circuits."

![Cartoon for the question: Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/009.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 9

### Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"?

**Folklore.** In May 1940 Churchill offered "blood, toil, tears and sweat." That is four items, not three, and "toil" is the word that dropped out.

Tell someone: Churchill offered "blood, toil, tears and sweat" in May 1940: four items, and "toil" is the word that dropped out.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- [Hansard, HC Deb 13 May 1940](https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1940/may/13/his-majestys-government-1)

Cited in the book: Hansard, HC Deb 13 May 1940. "Rule of three (writing)," Wikipedia. "Tricolon," Wikipedia.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/010.png)

DISPUTED

Round 1 · No. 10

### Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"?

**Disputed.** A maxim like it came out of an Air Force rocket-sled project around 1949, and Murphy's name stuck to it. Who first said it, and in what words, is not settled. The earliest firm printing under Murphy's name, from 1952, credits an unnamed physicist.

Tell someone: Who first said Murphy's law is disputed; its earliest firm printing under his name, in 1952, credits an unnamed physicist.

The book's full answer was checked on 12 November 2026 against

- ["Murphy's law," Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murphy%27s_law)

Cited in the book: Spark, *A History of Murphy's Law* (2006). "The Real-Life Murphy and How 'Murphy's Law' Came to Be," Military.com. Roe, *The Making of a Scientist* (1952).

## Answer key

1. Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath? **FOLKLORE**
2. Did an apple fall on Newton's head? **FOLKLORE**
3. Did Newton himself tell the apple story? **TRUE**
4. Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa? **FOLKLORE**
5. Did Pythagoras discover the Pythagorean theorem? **FOLKLORE**
6. Did Einstein write E = mc² in his 1905 paper? **FOLKLORE**
7. Did Einstein win his Nobel Prize for something other than relativity? **TRUE**
8. Did Gordon Moore say chips double every 18 months? **FOLKLORE**
9. Did Churchill promise "blood, sweat and tears"? **FOLKLORE**
10. Did Edward Murphy say "Anything that can go wrong will go wrong"? **DISPUTED**

That was round 1 of 10

## Nine more rounds are in the book.

The book has the full answer to every story: the real version, why the myth spread and the earliest source. Rounds 2 to 10 cover who really said it, famous experiments, charts and numbers, misleading names, kitchen physics, phrases, jokes that became laws, discovery stories, and money and power.

## Can you call the first three?

Make a call to start

![Cartoon for the question: Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/001.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 1

### Did Archimedes shout "Eureka!" in the bath?

**Folklore.** Archimedes stated the law of buoyancy around 250 BC, in his treatise *On Floating Bodies*. The bath, the crown and the cry of "Eureka!" are almost certainly a later embellishment.

![Cartoon for the question: Did an apple fall on Newton's head?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/002.png)

FOLKLORE

Round 1 · No. 2

### Did an apple fall on Newton's head?

**Folklore.** There is an apple in Newton's own account of his thinking about gravity. It does not hit him on the head. That detail is a later embellishment.

![Cartoon for the question: Did Newton himself tell the apple story?](https://conyso.com/publishing/art/003.png)

TRUE

Round 1 · No. 3

### Did Newton himself tell the apple story?

**True.** The apple story is not a fable invented by Newton's admirers. According to *Encyclopaedia Britannica*, it traces back to Newton's own later recollection. Only the apple hitting his head was added afterward.

[Play all of round 1](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore-round-1.html)

## Did Newton get hit by an apple? Did Archimedes really shout "Eureka!" in the bath? Did Galileo drop balls from the Leaning Tower?

Everyone has heard these stories. Fewer people know which ones actually happened.

**True or Folklore?** puts 100 famous stories from science, history, money and the mind to the test. Each one starts as a question on its own page, with a cartoon and three boxes to tick: **TRUE**, **FOLKLORE** or **DISPUTED**. Then turn the page for the verdict, the real story, why the myth spread, and the earliest source that settles it.

### The gift

- A page at the front to write who it's for
- Score titles from "Easily Fooled" to "Myth Buster" to argue over
- A "Tell someone" fact at the end of every answer, for the next dinner conversation

### What they'll keep using

- **100 stories in 10 ready-made quiz rounds** for game nights, with a two-team scoresheet
- **Two minutes per story**, so it works for a commute or a coffee break
- **Every verdict checked against the record**, with the source named on the page. Eighteen stories are still genuinely disputed, and the book says so
- A page of ideas for using it in class

48 FOLKLORE

34 TRUE

18 DISPUTED

## What's inside the ten rounds?

1. Round 1 **Famous scenes** The stories everyone has heard. A warm-up.
2. Round 2 **Who really said it?** Lines pinned on the wrong person, or on nobody in particular.
3. Round 3 **Famous experiments, retold** What the textbook version leaves out.
4. Round 4 **Charts and numbers** Famous pictures and figures, checked against the original.
5. Round 5 **Names that mislead** Laws named after people who did not find them, and odder naming stories.
6. Round 6 **Physics in the kitchen and the sky** Everyday science myths.
7. Round 7 **Words and phrases** Where the famous expressions really come from.
8. Round 8 **Jokes that became laws** Satire, office humor and asides that hardened into rules.
9. Round 9 **Discovery stories** Who found what, and how the credit was shared out.
10. Round 10 **Money, power and policy** Bounties, bombs and bad incentives.

## Where do the stories come from?

The Law Tome series is built from [the Law Tome](https://conyso.com/lawtome/), a free, sourced directory of 1,116 named laws, effects and principles; each story names its source on the page and links to its law. [How we make books](https://conyso.com/publishing/how-we-make-books.html) and [how we use AI](https://conyso.com/publishing/how-we-use-ai.html) explain the rest. Corrections found after print are listed on the [corrections page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/errata/).

Not on sale yet, so there is no store link or price here. The day it is, this page and [the Law Tome's books page](https://conyso.com/lawtome/books/) will link to it.

## Questions about the book

Who is True or Folklore? for?

Anyone who likes being the person who knows the real version: quiz hosts, family tables, classrooms and curious readers. It is written as a gift, with a page at the front to write who it is for.

How long does each story take?

About two minutes. The question sits alone on one page and the answer is printed on the back.

How many of the stories are true?

34 of the 100. 48 are folklore, and 18 are still genuinely disputed, which the book says rather than pretending to settle.

What age is it for?

Adults and teens. Round 3 (famous experiments) includes a murder and psychology experiments that harmed people, and rounds 7 and 10 touch on war and nuclear strategy, so read those rounds before using them with younger students.

Can I try it before it is out?

Yes. [Round 1](https://conyso.com/publishing/true-or-folklore-round-1.html) is free to play here, with each story's verdict and the sources it was checked against.

What formats will it come in?

Paperback and Kindle. In the Kindle edition each answer is behind a link from its question. There is no store link yet because it is not on sale yet.
